topic: Kimi K3.1 Pro: 1.56 TB of open weights vs the machines you own
title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Is Free. Running It Isn't.
description: Kimi K3.1 Pro open weights: 1.56 TB of MXFP4 against a DGX Spark, a Mac Studio and a 24 GB card. You will learn what actually fits, what the community quants change, and what to run tonight. Full channel: https://youtube.com/@BuildLocalAI (Narration is AI-generated.)
hook_candidates: You download the new frontier model. Then you see the size.
One point five six terabytes of open weights, too big for your machine.
Kimi K3.1 Pro is free. Your memory is not.
1.56 TB of weights just landed. Nothing on your desk holds them.
The first frontier open-weights drop fits no gaming PC.
Your DGX Spark has 128 GB. This model needs 1.56 TB.
Free model, one and a half terabytes, no desk holds it.
Moonshot shipped a model you cannot run. Here's the math.
Too big for a 4090. Too big for a Spark. Quantize.
You want it local. It weighs one point five six terabytes.
Kimi K3.1 Pro: free download, can't run.
narration_full: Kimi K three point one Pro: free download, can't run. You've seen the claim behind every open-weights drop: the model is free, so anyone can run it. And the download really is free, sitting on Hugging Face right now. Here's what free weighs: one point five six terabytes of weights. That's storage, space on a drive. The big expert weights ship four-bit, a compression the model was trained to expect. Everything outside them ships bigger, so the total on Moonshot's page looks like this. Moonshot built it as a mixture-of-experts model, hundreds of specialist networks with a receptionist that wakes only the few each word needs. And the receptionist re-picks every word, not once per thought. Speed comes from the activated parameters, the few that wake. The memory bill comes from all of them. Now hold that against your hardware. A top gaming card carries twenty-four gigabytes of video memory. That's about one part in sixty of the download. NVIDIA's DGX Spark, a desktop box built for serious local models, holds less than a tenth. The biggest Mac Studio Apple sells still holds only about a third. So the honest version is smaller. The download is free. The memory to hold it is not. No machine you own comes close, not NVIDIA's DGX Spark, not Apple's Mac Studio. A community quant, a third-party re-encode at fewer bits, is the usual escape. None exists for this model yet. The previous model's smallest squeeze was five hundred ninety-four gigabytes of weights. That's bigger than any Mac, and it agrees with the original about four fifths of the time. There's disk offload, streaming experts from a fast drive as each word needs them. It works. It crawls. Until a quant exists, renting it from Moonshot's API costs less than the drive you'd buy just to hold it. The weights are free. The machine that runs them isn't.
